newsitem.title: USA: U.S. military uses long reach against Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.S. military uses long reach against Iraq.

text.p: The U.S. military on Tuesday again used the long, powerful sting of computer-brain cruise missiles against Iraq to avoid casualties to American pilots from Saddam Hussein's air defenses.

It was the third time since the start of the 1991 Gulf War that the Pentagon has used Tomahawk and other "smart" missiles capable of hitting targets from more than 500 miles (800 km) away without risking American pilots over enemy territory.

The low-flying missiles, guided by computer chips and satellites, were used against Baghdad and other heavily defended targets in the 1991 war, again in 1993 to destroy an intelligence headquarters in Baghdad and then on Tuesday against air defense facilities in southern Iraq.
Defense Secretary William Perry told a Pentagon news conference the 27 missiles were fired from two U.S. warships in the Gulf and from B-52 bombers to avoid casualties to American pilots.

"We have many options for how we conduct a mission like this," he said. "We considered many of those options. One of the great advantages of the cruise missiles is the minimal risk to the U.S. forces involved."

Perry said the decision to launch 14 Tomahawk missiles from warships in the Gulf and 13 air-launched cruise missiles (AGMs) from B-52 bombers flying far from Iraq "was a choice of convenience, not of necessity."

He and Air Force Gen. Joseph Ralston, vice chairman of the U.S. military Joint Chiefs of Staff, said the two types of missiles were used against different targets. The Tomahawk, an advanced version of the weapon used from warships during the Gulf War, carries 1,000-pound (454 kg) warheads. The AGM carries 2,000-pound (908 kg) warheads to blast through heavier concrete.
Defense officials said the 18-foot (5.6-meter) long Tomahawks used on Tuesday are electronically guided by satellites circling the earth so they can strike close to the target.

"What you have here is a weapon that can be very, very effective against static targets such as air defense radars, anti-aircraft missile sites and other points," said one senior Pentagon official privately. "The things are very expensive, but there is really no choice when it comes to risking a pilot or spending a million bucks."
